name: opuspp
workload: Decoding a 60 s mixed-audio stream (tones, noise, transients, orchestral music) encoded by libopus at 320 kb/s, complexity 4, fullband stereo, 10 ms CELT frames (OPUS_APPLICATION_RESTRICTED_CELT, prediction disabled), 48 kHz float output; best of 7 passes, one pinned core, packet buffer flushed from cache before each pass.
claimed_speedup: 1.27x to 1.48x faster like for like (same compiler, same flags) at 320 kb/s; 1.09x to 1.50x across other bit rates (128, 510 kb/s), 10% packet loss and encoder complexities 0 and 4; five of six opuspp builds beat the fastest libopus build (GCC Fast) by 1.33x to 1.43x, while the GCC -Os build is 0.88x of it.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 16.2 and Clang 22.1, identical flags for libopus and opuspp: Size -Os; Balanced -O2; Fast -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -falign-loops=32 (libopus built with OPUS_FLOAT_APPROX=ON and OPUS_FAST_MATH=ON in Fast); all with -DNDEBUG -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -Wl,--gc-sections
stars_or_usage: 0 stars; repository has a single commit (created 2026-10-02)
tradeoffs: Specialised decoder, not a general Opus decoder: CELT-only, fullband, 10 ms frames, 48 kHz stereo float, prediction disabled, no SILK, hybrid, FEC or pitch post-filter. Header-only freestanding C++23, no heap allocation, no libm. Decoder state 18.1 KB vs 26.6 KB; code 71-198 KB vs 98-236 KB static libopus. Bit-identical to libopus in Size and Balanced builds; the Fast profile (-ffast-math) is not bit-exact in either decoder.
caveats: Code was written by Claude Code (the README says so) and the repo has one commit and no users yet. Gains are for the one stream configuration it supports. Benchmark source (opuspp/tests/bench.cpp, opuspp/tools/profile_report.py) is public and was opened; the numbers were not re-run. libopus is linked statically; the author reports the shared libopus performs on par with static.
found_via: WebSearch: 'faster than libopus OR faster than Opus audio codec encoder decoder implementation benchmark github' led to Rust ports; github.com/topics/audio-codec?l=c++ listed mhaugstrup/opuspp-ai-port ('header-only, freestanding C++23 port of the libopus 1.6.1 decoder')

name: dav1d
workload: Decoding 3840x2160 60 fps AV1 (about 10 Mbps, low-delay P) clips, 'game' (1200 frames) and 'camera' (1094 frames), at 4 to 6 threads, measured by a third party in a pull request to OvenMediaEngine.
claimed_speedup: libaom 3.12.0 vs dav1d 1.5.4: 22.3 fps vs 74.7 fps (about 3.3x) at 4 threads on the game clip; 22.1 fps vs 67.6 fps (about 3.1x) at 6 threads on the camera clip. The PR summarises 'about 3x faster'. Snippet only (CNX Software / blog posts, pages not opened): single-threaded 1.5-2.5x and multi-threaded 2.3-4.5x faster than libaom, about one quarter of libaom's memory.
hardware: 2x Intel Xeon Silver 4114 @ 2.20 GHz (20C/40T, AVX2/AVX-512), 48 GB DDR4-2400, Ubuntu 22.04.5, performance governor
stars_or_usage: 807 stars on the GitHub mirror (canonical repo is code.videolan.org/videolan/dav1d); decoder widely used via FFmpeg (libdav1d)
tradeoffs: Decoder only. Hand-written assembly for x86 (SSSE3 and up, AVX2) and ARM (ARMv7, ARMv8); the README says it is written from scratch for speed, size and correctness. Snippet only: binary about one third the size of libaom's decoder.
caveats: The numbers come from a third-party PR description, not a benchmark suite: build flags, assembly settings and the exact command are not stated and no script is linked. The dav1d README itself carries no numbers. The Xeon Silver 4114 is an old CPU. Multi-core scaling figures are from one machine.
found_via: WebSearch: 'dav1d decoder speed benchmark paper fps compared to libaom libgav1 decoding performance table' surfaced OvenMediaEngine PR #2336; first query 'fast video encoding decoding paper speed faster than x265 libaom dav1d open source encoder' surfaced videolan/dav1d

name: VVenC
baseline: HM (HEVC reference encoder) and VTM-19.2 (VVC reference encoder)
workload: Encoding JVET HD and UHD test sequences with five presets (faster to slower), 8 threads, version 1.14.0; speed measured relative to the HM reference encoder, bit-rate saving as PSNR BD-rate vs HM.
claimed_speedup: Table III (v1.14.0, 8 threads), speedup vs HM with BD-rate vs HM: faster 360x HD / 400x UHD at -11.2% / -15.0%; fast 170x / 190x at -24.8% / -26.6%; medium 43x / 62x at -34.1% / -36.0%; slow 11x / 16x at -38.3% / -39.9%; slower 2x / 4x at -41.2% / -42.8%. Wiki landing page: 'between 20x and 2400x over VTM-19.2 for HD and UHD test sequences depending on the chosen quality/speed preset'.
hardware: Dell servers with AMD EPYC 7502P 32-core @ 2.5 GHz (stated for v1.7.0 onward)
tradeoffs: Encodes H.266/VVC, a different (newer) codec from x265/HEVC; needs a VVC decoder (vvdec, OpenVVC, or others). BSD-3-Clause-Clear explicitly grants no patent licence. Five presets, frame-level parallelism, XPSNR-based perceptual optimisation.
caveats: Baselines (HM, VTM) are reference encoders, not x264/x265. A comparison with x265 exists only as figures on the wiki and in the ICMEW 2021 and MM'21 papers by the authors (not opened, blocked); no x265 number is recorded here. Compiler and flags are not stated in the wiki tables. First-party numbers.
found_via: WebSearch: 'VVC decoder real-time open source vvdec OpenVVC paper decoding speed' and direct fetch of github.com/fraunhoferhhi/vvenc and its wiki

name: SVT-AV1
baseline: libaom (AV1 reference encoder); the changelog also positions presets against x265 medium and x264 veryfast
workload: AV1 encoding on multi-core servers across presets M0 to M13; quality/speed trade-off versus libaom, x265 and x264 as stated by the project.
claimed_speedup: CHANGELOG v0.8.7 (2021-05-08): 'Preset 8 achieving similar speed levels as x265 medium tuned for VOD operating mode'. CHANGELOG v0.9 (2022-01-19): 'New faster presets M9-M12, M12 reaching similar complexity level to that of x264 veryfast'. Snippet only (Netflix Tech Blog 2020 and third-party guides, pages blocked): similar compression efficiency to libaom with significantly lower encoding latency on multi-core platforms; third-party posts quote 10-50x faster than libaom.
stars_or_usage: 75 stars on the GitHub mirror; canonical repo on GitLab (5,270 commits, 45 releases); founded by Intel with Netflix and adopted by the Alliance for Open Media
tradeoffs: Encoder only. Faster presets give up compression efficiency; at the slowest presets it only reaches similar efficiency to libaom. Licensed BSD-3-Clause-Clear plus the AOM Patent License 1.0.
caveats: The numbers on the opened page are 'similar speed' statements, not a speedup ratio over libaom or x265. The libaom claim comes only from search snippets of blocked pages (snippet only). The README links peer-reviewed SPIE and ICIP papers (SPIE 2020 'The SVT-AV1 encoder: overview, features and speed-quality tradeoffs') that were not opened. Other changelog entries cite speed comparisons only against earlier SVT-AV1 versions on AWS Graviton4 with Clang 19/20.
found_via: WebSearch: 'SVT-AV1 paper scalable encoder faster than libaom speed compression efficiency tradeoff'; gitlab.com/AOMediaCodec/SVT-AV1 README and CHANGELOG.md

name: Kvazaar
workload: HEVC encoding at equal coding efficiency (BD-rate) versus x265; papers cover multi-core intra encoding, AVX2-optimised intra encoding, and an all-intra evaluation on Nvidia Jetson.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only (papers not opened): a C implementation of Kvazaar is 19% faster than x265 for the same coding efficiency with 8 threads and 38% faster with 16 threads (SiPS 2015 parallelisation paper); at high-speed presets Kvazaar has 4.5% better coding efficiency while twice as fast as x265; AVX2-optimised Kvazaar is 20% faster than AVX2-optimised x265 ultrafast with 9.1% bit-rate gain; Jetson all-intra evaluation (J. Real-Time Image Processing, 2024): Kvazaar is 65.44% and 69.4% faster than x265 with 1.88% and 0.6% BD-rate improvement at the high-speed and high-quality presets.
stars_or_usage: 966 stars; developed by the Ultravideo research group (Tampere University)
tradeoffs: HEVC encoder only; README states speed and RD quality 'will continue to improve'.
caveats: Snippet only: all numbers come from search-result snippets of blocked papers (SiPS 2015 'Parallelization of Kvazaar HEVC Intra Encoder for Multi-core Processors', 'AVX2-optimized Kvazaar HEVC intra encoder', 'Kvazaar HEVC encoder for efficient intra coding', 'Performance evaluation of all intra Kvazaar and x265 HEVC encoders on embedded system Nvidia Jetson platform'); x265 versions, presets and CPU models were not seen. The numbers span different years and x265 versions. The Kvazaar README itself carries no benchmark numbers.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Kvazaar HEVC encoder paper speed compared to x265 kvazaar faster at same bitrate BD-rate'

name: zimg
workload: Resizing a full-HD frame to UHD with a Lanczos filter, and converting full-HD BT.709 YUV to BT.2020, per-frame time in milliseconds.
claimed_speedup: FHD to UHD Lanczos resize: zimg 2.8 7.7 ms vs swscale 4.0.2 15.2 ms on Intel i7-8565U, 10.8 ms vs 22.2 ms on Xeon Platinum 8176. FHD BT.709 (YUV) to BT.2020: zimg 2.8 8.3 ms vs swscale 17.5 ms on i7-8565U, 11.5 ms vs 25.6 ms on Xeon Platinum 8176. About 2x (derived from page data).
hardware: Intel Core i7-8565U; Intel Xeon Platinum 8176
tradeoffs: Scaling, colour-space conversion and depth conversion only (no codecs); C API with C++ implementation, tuned for Intel SIMD. Different default filters and quality settings than swscale.
caveats: First-party README numbers from old versions (zimg 2.8, swscale 4.0.2); compiler, flags, swscale options and benchmark code are not stated. WTFPL is not OSI-listed but is a permissive dedication-style licence. The zscale remark comes from search results (FFmpeg zscale page), not from the opened README.
found_via: WebSearch: 'libyuv OR zimg faster than swscale benchmark scaling colorspace conversion speed comparison ffmpeg'

name: OpenVVC
baseline: VTM reference decoder and Fraunhofer VVdeC
workload: Software decoding of VVC (H.266) bit-streams on multi-core x86 and embedded ARM platforms; also a live 4K intra end-to-end pipeline paper.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only: OpenVVC decodes at over 290 fps for FHD and 90 fps for UHD on a multi-core x86 platform; compared with VTM and VVdeC it has a higher decoding rate with lower memory use, especially in all-intra; VVdeC needs 2x the memory of OpenVVC on both platforms; an end-to-end pipeline built around OpenVVC is almost 34,000 times as fast as the VTM pipeline and 3.3x faster than the fastest VVenC/VVdeC configuration (ACM MMSys 2023 toolkit paper).
tradeoffs: Supports 8-bit bit-streams, frame and tile parallelism, RPR; README says it is still under development. Lightweight, lower memory than VVdeC.
caveats: Snippet only: numbers are from search snippets of the arXiv 2205.12217 abstract and the ACM MMSys 2023 'Open-Source Toolkit for Live End-to-End 4K VVC Intra Coding' paper (both blocked, not opened); the repo README has no numbers. The baselines are VTM and VVdeC, not FFmpeg/x265. Last commit shown on the master commit page is 2022-03-22, so the code may be far behind the paper's decoder.
found_via: WebSearch: 'VVC decoder real-time open source vvdec OpenVVC paper decoding speed faster than libde265 VTM fps'

name: uavs3e
workload: AVS3 encoding (a different codec from HEVC) compared against x265 on compression (veryslow) and encoding speed (ultrafast) for up to 8K real-time encoding.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only: versus the x265 veryslow preset uavs3e gives average BD-rate savings of 22.7% (luma) and 46.1% / 46.2% (chroma); the uAVS3e RealTime encoder shows 'a significant advantage in encoding speed compared to x265' (no ratio seen) and is described as capable of real-time processing up to 8K.
stars_or_usage: 162 stars; Peking University Shenzhen Graduate School / Peng Cheng Laboratory
tradeoffs: Encodes AVS3-P2 baseline profile, not HEVC, so it is not a drop-in x265 replacement; SSE4/AVX2 and ARM paths; 10-bit support.
caveats: Snippet only: numbers come from search snippets of the IEEE paper 'An Efficient and Open Source Encoder Uavs3e for Video Compression' and a later real-time paper (blocked, not opened); the repo README has no numbers. The comparison crosses codecs (AVS3 vs HEVC). Licence is described as BSD 4-clause with custom copyright text, with an advertising clause. No speed ratio was seen.
found_via: WebSearch: 'xeve OR uavs3e OR xavs2 open-source encoder faster than x265 real-time paper benchmark speed BD-rate'

name: opus-rs
workload: Mono encode-only of real speech (fixtures/answer_16k.wav) at 8/16/48 kHz with 10 and 20 ms frames, VoIP and Audio applications; wall-clock time for the full frame set, Criterion with 20 samples.
claimed_speedup: Ryzen 7 5700X (x86-64, AVX2/FMA): 48 kHz/20 ms Audio 25.1 ms vs 28.4 ms (Rust 12% faster); 48 kHz/10 ms Audio 29.7 ms vs 31.2 ms (5% faster); 8 kHz/20 ms VoIP 39.9 ms vs 40.6 ms (2% faster); 16 kHz/10 ms VoIP 73.2 ms vs 72.5 ms (C 1% faster). Apple Silicon M-series (2026-04-23): 48 kHz/20 ms 13.97 ms vs 19.39 ms (Rust 28% faster); 48 kHz/10 ms 16.19 ms vs 20.28 ms (20% faster); 8 kHz/20 ms VoIP C 0.9% faster.
compiler_and_flags: cargo --release (opt-level=3 + ThinLTO); rustc version and libopus build flags not stated
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 5700X; Apple Silicon M-series (model not stated)
tradeoffs: Pure Rust port of libopus 1.6, #![no_std] with no alloc option; Rust only, so not callable from C++ without a C ABI wrapper. Most results are within a few percent of libopus; the README calls it 'competitive'.
caveats: The README tells readers to run `cargo bench --bench opus_vs_c_bench`, but that target is not in the repo: benches/ holds only opus_bench.rs (which has no libopus comparison), Cargo.toml registers only opus_bench, and bench_quick.sh refers to 'opus_vs_c_real', so the C comparison cannot be reproduced from the checked-in code. Some rows are within noise or favour C. Encode-only, mono, single speech clip; stereo and music are untested. Tier would be A if the C-comparison benchmark were public.
found_via: WebSearch: 'faster than libopus OR faster than Opus audio codec encoder decoder implementation benchmark github'

name: rusty-opus
baseline: libopus (C reference encoder); also FFmpeg's native Opus encoder
workload: Single-thread encode of 300 s and 150 s clips driven as processes, reporting the slope t(300 s) minus t(150 s), pinned to one core, CPU time, ABBA-interleaved, 31 reps, with a null arm; split by coding path verified from TOC bytes (CELT 48 kHz speech at 32k, CELT 48 kHz stereo music at 128k, SILK 16 kHz speech at 16k).
claimed_speedup: CELT speech 436x realtime vs libopus 291x (1.50x faster, FFmpeg native 310x); CELT stereo music 213x vs 133x (1.60x faster, FFmpeg native 71x); SILK 139x vs 145x (0.96x, libopus 4% ahead). Frame-parallel encoding adds wall-clock speedup on top. Quality: mean BD-ODG -0.015 vs libopus over 13 core classes (parity), +1.532 vs FFmpeg's native Opus encoder.
stars_or_usage: 5 stars, 4 forks; crates.io rusty-opus 0.9.1 with 34,214 downloads
tradeoffs: Pure Rust Opus encoder and decoder with hand-written AVX2/FMA and NEON kernels (unsafe confined to SIMD), runtime CPU detection; adds frame-parallel encoding with PEAQ-neutral seams. Rust only. Quality at parity with libopus except lower on VoIP-application speech and some stereo music classes.
caveats: First-party numbers. Compiler version and build flags are not stated, although the reproduction script tools/bench_encode_3way.ps1 is public (confirmed to exist, not run). The README's quality measurement uses PEAQ ODG on short public-domain clips and says so. The repo is a performance fork of restsend/opus-rs and part of the 'Remade With Rust' marketing initiative; the README opens with an install-count banner and an advert. Single laptop CPU.
found_via: WebSearch: 'faster than libopus OR faster than Opus audio codec encoder decoder implementation benchmark github'

name: remade_ffmpeg_rs
baseline: FFmpeg libavcodec native MP3 decoder and native AAC encoder; libvorbis
workload: MP3 decode of a 27.5-minute stream, decode-and-discard on the same physical cores, 15 pairs; AAC-LC encode of a 60 s stereo clip with frame-parallel encoding; Vorbis encode of stereo music on 24 cores.
claimed_speedup: MP3 decode 1.24x faster than FFmpeg on 1 core (1,952 vs 2,431 ms, 15/15 pairs) and 1.39x on 2 cores (1,017 vs 1,455 ms), at lower total CPU (1,875 vs 2,125 ms); AAC encode about 6x faster than ffmpeg's own AAC encoder via frame-parallel encoding (about 450x realtime; single-thread about 1.15x); Vorbis encode about 5.3x faster than libvorbis wall-clock (frame-parallel, 24 cores; per-thread about 1.4x behind libvorbis). Image side (not video-audio): PNG decode 2.55-2.89x faster than ffmpeg, lossy WebP decode 1.24-1.29x.
stars_or_usage: 6 stars; crates.io rusty_mp3 0.8.0 (42,200 downloads), rusty_aac 0.5.0, rusty_vorbis 0.1.1 point to this repo
tradeoffs: Pure-Rust 'FFmpeg remade' with permissive licences; codecs are also published as standalone crates (rusty_mp3, rusty_aac, rusty_vorbis, rusty_png, rusty_webp). Rust only. The AAC and Vorbis headline speedups come from multi-threaded frame-parallel encoding against single-threaded baselines. Video codecs are slower than the incumbents: VP9 decode about 0.16-0.21x of FFmpeg, VP9 encode about 0.3x at +36% bit rate, H.264 decode about 2x behind FFmpeg's native decoder, MP3 encoder about 0.7-1.1 ODG behind LAME on average (1.4-1.8 on transients).
caveats: First-party; hardware, compiler and flags are not stated for the audio rows and no benchmark script was seen on the opened README. The README itself notes an earlier CLI-to-CLI comparison had MP3 decode 1.20x behind and was corrected to a matched-core comparison. The repo carries CLAUDE.md and .claude directories (AI-assisted). The crates rusty_mp3, rusty_aac, rusty_vorbis share this repo URL, so any standalone listing needs a paper: id to avoid duplicates. Only the README text was read; the code was not.
found_via: WebSearch: 'faster than libopus OR faster than Opus audio codec ...' returned rusty-opus, whose README links remade_ffmpeg_rs; crates.io API for rusty_aac / rusty_mp3 / rusty_vorbis (repository field)

name: SuperLAME
workload: Encoding a 44-minute album to CBR 320 kb/s MP3, 2 to 16 threads, in-RAM benchmark mode.
claimed_speedup: 'Roughly 8x faster than stock single-threaded LAME at the same quality'; Ryzen 7 5800X3D, v1.1.0: 13.8 s at 2 threads down to 3.9 s at 16 threads (about 680x realtime); parallel efficiency about 93% at 2 workers and about 61% at 16.
compiler_and_flags: clang++ -std=c++17 -O2 -march=x86-64 for the frontend, clang -O2 for dr_flac, plus four libmp3lame engine builds (znver5, znver4, znver3, SSE2) in one binary; Windows executable
tradeoffs: Runs many libmp3lame instances in parallel on chunks and repairs the bit reservoir, so the gain is thread parallelism. Single-thread output is bit-identical to stock LAME; multi-thread output differs by an inaudible (below -45 dB) reconciliation at chunk seams. Whole input and output are held in RAM (about 1-2 GB input limit). Needs clang to build the SIMD paths; GPL because it combines LGPL LAME and mpg123 with GPL code ported from fre:ac/BoCA.
caveats: First-party README numbers; the stock-LAME timing that the 8x is measured against is not shown on the page, and the 8x applies to multi-threaded use on a many-core desktop. A --bench mode and tests/scaling.ps1 are described (not opened or run). Very new repo (July 2026) with 3 stars. Windows-oriented.
found_via: WebSearch: 'HALAC lossless audio codec github faster than FLAC OR SuperLAME multithreaded MP3 encoder 8x faster than LAME github'

name: Shine
workload: Encoding a 5:18 stereo 44.1 kHz 16-bit WAV to 128 kb/s MP3 on an M1 Pro MacBook Pro (December 2022); older runs on Raspberry Pi and Nexus 5.
claimed_speedup: M1 Pro: Shine 318.0x realtime vs LAME 88.7x realtime (about 3.6x, derived from page data). Raspberry Pi (marked outdated): Shine 3.6x realtime vs LAME 3.99.5 1.8x realtime (about 2x, derived). Nexus 5: Shine 24.2x realtime.
hardware: Apple M1 Pro MacBook Pro (arm64); Raspberry Pi (ARM, FPU); Google Nexus 5
stars_or_usage: 422 stars; ships JavaScript/WebAssembly and Android bindings; encoder CLI is the 'Liquidsoap version'
tradeoffs: Fixed-point MP3 encoder meant for CPUs without an FPU. It has no psychoacoustic model, so quality per bit is lower than LAME, and the README warns it may contain bugs. Simple algorithm.
caveats: First-party README timings pasted from terminal output; compiler flags, build type and the quality side of the comparison are not given. LAME ran at its default quality (qval=3), so this compares a lower-quality fast encoder against LAME's default. COPYING is the GNU Library GPL v2 text; the SPDX id is inferred from that header. Last commits are from 2023-01-01. The README text was read through the toots/shine path, which the README says is the same project as savonet/shine.
found_via: WebSearch: 'dr_flac benchmark faster than libFLAC decoding speed dr_mp3 minimp3 faster than libmpg123 ffmpeg' led to checking MP3 codec READMEs; direct raw fetch of toots/shine README and github.com/savonet/shine

name: rusty-av1-toolkit
baseline: stock rav1e (AV1 encoder); decoder side is a fork of rav1d, itself a Rust port of dav1d
workload: Whole-encode wall-clock of the forked rav1e encoder against stock rav1e through the real CLI, A/B on the author's machine.
claimed_speedup: Default mode (--racecar off): about 1.10x faster with a byte-identical bit-stream to stock rav1e; opt-in --racecar on: about 1.69x faster (bit-stream changes, pair with --tune Psnr). Decoder: 'same as rav1d, profiled at its performance floor' (no speedup claim).
tradeoffs: Encoder fork of rav1e (not a GitHub fork: the parent code is vendored into rusty_av1e/) with tuned hot kernels and asm; the content-adaptive 'RAV1E_FAST=fast' tier trades quality for speed and is content-dependent (measured +5.3% bus, +3.3% akiyo, -8.7% mobile BD-rate vs the default at speed 6). Rust only; the baseline is rav1e, not libaom, SVT-AV1 or x265.
caveats: First-party; hardware, clips, rustc version, flags and run counts are not stated for the speed ratios ('on this machine'). No ratio against libaom, dav1d or x265 is given. Part of the Remade With Rust initiative, AI-assisted repo. Moderate value: a ~10% gain over rav1e at identical output.
found_via: crates.io search of the Remade With Rust family listed in the rusty-opus README; github.com/Remade-With-Rust/rusty-av1-toolkit README
